passage:
A message arrived on a rainy Tuesday in Toronto: "Dalia? It's Siddiq. I know it's been six years. I've thought about you a lot." Dalia read it standing in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in her hand. Pleased, first, in a rush. Then wary, then a small hot flicker of resentment: six years of birthdays without a word, and now this.

She put the spoon down and typed, "It's really good to hear from you. I'll be honest, I was hurt when we lost touch. I'd like to catch up, slowly."

Siddiq answered within minutes, apologising for going silent after the move and asking how her mother was. They arranged a video call for Saturday. Dalia didn't pretend the gap wasn't there, and she didn't plan a lecture. She would see who showed up.

qa.q: How many years had passed since Siddiq last got in touch?
qa.a: Siddiq wrote, 'I know it's been six years.'

qa.q: What did Dalia feel on reading the message?
qa.a: Pleased first, then wary, then a small flicker of resentment about the years of silence.

qa.q: How did Dalia reply, and why does it help?
qa.a: She said it was good to hear from Siddiq, named the hurt honestly and asked to catch up slowly, which neither hides the gap nor punishes.

qa.q: How might Siddiq have felt when sending the first message?
qa.a: Probably nervous about being turned away, since Siddiq apologised quickly for the silence once Dalia answered.

grounding: An old friend reaches out after years; Dalia feels pleased, wary and a little resentful and meets it with honest warmth, letting trust return slowly.

passage:
Santosh,

Your message came on Tuesday, and I've read it maybe twenty times. "Sid, I know it's been six years. I've missed you. Can we meet?"

I want to be honest, because I think that's the only way this works. My first feeling was happiness. I actually laughed out loud in the metro. My second was something harder. When my father was in hospital in 2020, I called you and you never called back. I waited a long time for that call.

I'm not writing this to punish you. I don't need an explanation today. But I can't pretend the six years didn't happen, and I don't think you'd want me to.

So yes, let's meet. Sunday, at the old Irani café near college? Let's have chai and see who we are now. Maybe it'll be easy. Maybe it'll take a few Sundays. I'm willing to find out.

Siddharth

qa.q: How many years had passed since Santosh and Siddharth were in touch?
What mix of feelings did Siddharth have about Santosh's message?
qa.a: Siddharth felt happy first, then a harder hurt and some resentment about the unanswered call years ago.

qa.q: How does Siddharth balance warmth and honesty in the reply?
qa.a: Siddharth agrees to meet warmly, names the old hurt plainly without punishing, and lets trust rebuild over a few Sundays.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel reading this reply?
qa.a: Santosh may feel relieved to be welcomed and a little ashamed about the missed call, but grateful for the honesty.

grounding: A letter shows someone whose old friend reaches out after six years, feeling pleased, wary and a little resentful, who replies with warmth and honesty and lets trust return slowly.

passage:
You want to know about Damini? Okay. I'm Omkar, and this is the story of the girl who vanished and came back.

We were best friends through engineering. After graduation she moved to Hyderabad, got engaged, and just... faded. Four years. Not even a reply to my birthday wishes.

Then last month: "Omkar, I'm in Pune this weekend. Coffee? I owe you an explanation."

I was thrilled, honestly. I was also angry, which surprised me. Part of me wanted to reply "Oh, NOW you remember me?"

I didn't. I went. She told me her engagement had ended badly and she'd pulled away from everyone. I listened. Then I said, "I'm really glad you're here. And it hurt, when you disappeared." She said, "I know. I'm sorry."

We're texting again, carefully. I'm not pretending the gap wasn't there. I'm not making her pay for it either. We're just going slow.

qa.q: How long had Damini been out of touch?
qa.a: She had been out of touch for four years.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel when Damini's message arrived?
qa.a: Omkar felt thrilled and, surprisingly, angry too, tempted to reply sarcastically.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's choices at the coffee meeting helped, and why?
qa.a: Omkar listened to Damini's reasons, said it was good to have her back, and honestly named that her disappearing hurt, without punishing her.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt coming to meet Omkar?
qa.a: Damini was probably nervous and ashamed, knowing she owed Omkar an explanation after four years.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone whose old friend returns after years, feeling pleased, wary and a little resentful, meeting her with warmth and honesty and letting trust return slowly.
